finding.claim: The user identity is taken straight from the client-supplied request header X-Session-User-Verified. Nothing in the code authenticates it (no session, signature or token check) or strips it. Every ACL decision depends on g.user, so any caller can impersonate any user who holds grants. That includes the delete and write permissions on /files/<fid> and /files/<fid>/rename. This assumes the app is reachable directly, or sits behind a proxy that does not overwrite or strip this header. Neither is enforced in this code.
finding.source: HTTP request header X-Session-User-Verified, set by any unauthenticated client
finding.sink: ensure_allowed/is_allowed in acl.py:5 and :8-10, guarding `del STORE[fid]` (views.py:18) and `f["name"] = ...` (views.py:27)

trace.note: before_request sets g.user from the raw header with no verification
is_allowed only checks whether the claimed user name is in resource grants, so a spoofed owner name passes
rename_file uses the same spoofed g.user for the write check

finding.guards_checked: Searched the repo's two files (acl.py, views.py) for any signature, session, JWT or proxy-trust check on the header and found none. The ACL check itself is enforced on both routes: delete_file calls ensure_allowed and aborts, and rename_file returns 403. But it trusts the spoofable identity. A missing header gives g.user=None, which is denied unless grants has a None key. This does not stop an attacker who names a real grantee.

verdict.guard_found: ACL checks only: ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, aborts 403) at views.py:17 and is_allowed (acl.py:5) tested at views.py:25. Both are enforced correctly, but they trust g.user. No signature, session, or header-stripping check exists in the repo.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: views.py:11 sets g.user from the raw header, and the ACL checks at views.py:17 and views.py:25 use it. Whether an anonymous client can reach this depends on whether an upstream proxy strips or overwrites X-Session-User-Verified. The header name suggests one does, but that is outside the available code, so exploitability can't be decided.
